sections.title: Build a gradient from an ordinary slope
paragraphs: For one number, a derivative is the local slope of a function. If \(f(a)=a^2\), moving a tiny amount epsilon changes the score by approximately \(2a\varepsilon\). At \(a=3\), the slope is 6: a step of 0.01 changes the score by about 0.06. The exact change is \(3.01^2-3^2=0.0601\). The approximation improves as the step becomes smaller.

For a vector, hold all but one coordinate fixed and take a slope for each coordinate. Those partial derivatives form the gradient. Let \(f(h)=h_1^2+3h_2\), where \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) are the first and second coordinates. At \(h=[2,1]\), \(f=7\) and the gradient is \(g=[4,3]\). For \(\delta=[0.1,-0.2]\), the dot product \(g\cdot\delta=4\times0.1+3\times(-0.2)=-0.2\) predicts the score change. The exact new score is \(2.1^2+3\times0.8=6.81\), a change of −0.19.

In general, for a scalar score f evaluated from a vector h, a small displacement \(\delta\) has approximate effect \(f(h+\delta)-f(h)\approx g\cdot\delta\), where \(g=\nabla_h f(h)\) is the gradient at \(h\). Each partial derivative holds the other coordinates fixed. This formula summarizes the local calculation illustrated above; it does not guarantee the same accuracy for a large patch.
\[f(h+\delta)-f(h)\approx\nabla_h f(h)\cdot\delta\]

Backpropagation computes such derivatives through composed operations using the chain rule: local sensitivities multiply along a route, and contributions add where routes meet. It is an efficient calculation of sensitivity to the chosen scalar score. It does not infer the meaning of that score or the scientific value of changing it.

The local approximation can fail for large moves or curved functions. At \(a=0\), \(f(a)=a^2\) has slope zero, but moving to \(a=1\) changes f by 1. Saturated output probabilities can likewise have small local slopes. AtP* addresses important failure modes in approximate patching; exact intervention checks remain necessary.

visual.caption: An original differentiable toy function. A gradient predicts a local score change; it does not label a coordinate as a scientific concept.

sections.title: Detection is not intervention
paragraphs: A label is the known outcome used for comparison, such as which task an example belongs to. Supervision means using these supplied labels or target answers to fit a method. A probe is an additional predictor trained on saved model states to predict a label. If a probe succeeds, the states contain information the probe can use; it does not follow that the original model uses the same predictor or that changing its inputs will improve the answer.

A feature that predicts a label need not be a useful control knob. The targeted feature-learning study compares activation values and gradient signals with different estimators, finding different strengths for detection and intervention. Its targets provide supervision and its intervention scores concern target-token probabilities. Free scientific generation is a further test.

Every fitted encoder, probe, reward model or selected direction adds an artifact and a selection procedure to the system. Record training data, target information, validation choices and compute. Novel currently implements a bounded selected-activation gradient diagnostic, not donor learning or a trained attribution pipeline. A nonzero gradient establishes local numerical sensitivity only.

sections.title: Identical prefixes imply identical pre-answer states in this setup
paragraphs: With the same complete condition—model, token IDs, positions, mask, numerical execution, stochastic operations and intervention state—a deterministic frozen computation produces the same pre-answer activations. A nonzero contrast must come from some changed part of that condition or a later answer-conditioned state. The visible wording alone does not establish identical inputs.

sections.title: Reading the four method families together
paragraphs: Function Vectors extracts task-related signals from demonstrations and tests transfer. Contrastive Activation Addition constructs contrasts from paired answer-conditioned examples and adds a direction at inference. AtP* uses derivatives to approximate which exact component patches matter. Targeted Feature Learning compares signals and estimators for detecting a target and changing its probability. These methods differ in what is extracted, what supervision is used and what outcome is measured.

A detector asks whether a state helps predict a label. A controller asks whether changing that state improves the desired outcome. A thermometer can detect heat without being a heater. For Novel, a transferable mechanism would need to improve relevant free-generation outcomes on separately held events with different answers, while surviving comparisons against text assistance and other donors. Current selected-activation gradients are a bounded diagnostic, not that completed pipeline.

chapters.takeaway: Audit where a direction got its information, then test transfer and selectivity independently.

chapters.title: Search, perturbation and useful scientific yield
chapters.summary: Disentangle noise, search, selection and extra training before claiming improved discovery.
chapters.whyNow: Diversity matters only if it produces more valid, useful work within a fair total budget.

sections.title: Separate generating, choosing and checking
paragraphs: A search procedure generates candidates, decides where to try next or which candidate to keep, and checks its output. Ordinary sampling changes the next chosen token. An activation perturbation changes intermediate numerical states. Weight steering changes the transformation parameters. A verifier scores candidates, while a selector uses available information to choose among them. These components can be combined, but each introduces a distinct source of assistance and cost.

Consider an invented comparison. System A generates one answer. System B generates ten answers and gives all of them to an expert. If B returns more valid ideas, we have evidence about the larger procedure. To isolate a proposed noise method, compare it with ordinary sampling using the same candidate budget, selection information and accounting rules. Otherwise more search or better review could explain the gain.

Diversity means variation according to a declared measure: wording, mechanisms or valid solutions can each vary differently. Ten colorful paraphrases may contain one idea. Ten different but invalid proposals may have high diversity and no scientific yield. Useful yield requires validity and usefulness as well as variation.

sections.title: More variation is not yet more science
paragraphs: Ordinary token sampling changes selected tokens. Internal perturbation changes a representation used to produce later tokens. Weight steering changes the transformation itself. Each creates a different system, even if all are called inference-time methods. A wider variety of sentences can be invalid, irrelevant or merely cosmetic.

Gaussian perturbation means adding a random vector whose coordinates follow a specified bell-shaped distribution, often centered at zero with a chosen standard deviation. Standard deviation describes scale: larger values typically produce larger coordinate changes. Correlation between coordinates, injection site, normalization and duration also matter. “Add noise” therefore names a family of interventions, not one reproducible method.

Soft Reasoning combines embedding exploration with verifier-guided optimization. Noise Steering studies constrained educational story generation. CreativityNeuro rescales selected weights and studies divergent thinking with human ratings. These are concrete methodological leads, but their task outcomes are not measurements of historical scientific reconstruction. CreativityNeuro’s reported utility and factual-competence tradeoffs make separate outcome dimensions particularly important.

sections.title: Separate the components of a claimed gain
paragraphs: A useful comparison might include ordinary sampling, prompting variants, clean refinement, random perturbation, and adaptive perturbation search. Give them equal selection information and a justified total compute budget. If the perturbation arm gets a verifier while the baseline does not, the intervention comparison also includes verification. If an oracle sees hidden correctness labels, that is an oracle-assisted condition.

Bayesian optimization uses outcomes from previous candidates to choose future candidates under a statistical surrogate. Those candidates are dependent on the search history; they are not independent draws from the original frozen decoder. Do not apply the original per-draw binomial analysis to an adaptive search process without defining a new endpoint and analysis.

Latent reasoning here means working with internal numerical states rather than expressing every step as readable text. GTS and LatentTTS are context readings only here. Their abstracts describe learned sampling or reward components around latent reasoning. A frozen backbone does not mean the whole system is training-free. Any attempted reuse would need an audit of its architecture, training objective, data sources and compatibility.

sections.title: What adaptive search learns between attempts
paragraphs: Bayesian optimization builds a statistical surrogate: a model of how candidate settings relate to previously observed scores, including uncertainty about untried settings. An acquisition rule uses that surrogate to choose another candidate, balancing predicted promise and information gain. Here the candidates might be perturbation directions or scales. The search is using feedback, so later attempts depend on earlier outcomes.

A verifier may check code tests, mathematical consistency or a learned reward, each with different blind spots. Optimizing a proxy can find candidates that exploit those blind spots. Keep the search objective separate from independent final evaluation and count the cost of learning or tuning the surrogate. A frozen language-model backbone can still sit inside a system with newly trained sampler or reward components.

Soft Reasoning combines continuous embedding exploration with verifier-guided search. Noise Steering studies constrained Arabic stories, and CreativityNeuro alters weights for divergent-thinking tasks. GTS and LatentTTS introduce learned latent sampling or reward components. They are methodological leads for later decisions; their benchmarks do not already measure Novel’s historical reconstruction endpoint. The library identifies the access depth and limitations of each.

Independent repetitions of the whole frozen search procedure could support a new endpoint, such as the chance that one complete search returns a valid proposal within its total budget. Its internal candidates remain history-dependent. This separates evaluating a complete adaptive system from pretending that all its internal trials came from the original frozen decoder.

sections.title: Recovery policy is an experimental factor
paragraphs: After a temporary perturbation, retaining the altered KV history, cleanly re-prefilling the same emitted text, and asking for a fresh clean refinement preserve different information. Declare each policy and compare it to its own no-noise control. Noise removal cannot undo an earlier sampled claim that now appears in the visible text.

Only proceed after G5: a specific hypothesis, selective predictions, development-chosen settings, new held-out event families, reliable outcomes and full cost accounting. NNsight can help express interventions, but its API and release claims do not validate a particular Qwen3 backend. Tool choice follows the experiment and its checks.

A successful later study would show more independently validated useful proposals per declared compute and review budget, with preserved unrelated competence and a replicated effect. Prospective discovery then adds contemporary prior-art review and domain-specific validation. That is the long-term destination; the current repository supplies the engineering and protocol groundwork.

chapters.takeaway: Attribute improvement to a complete, controlled procedure, and keep validity and utility alongside diversity.

glossary.definition: A vocabulary item represented by an integer ID; it need not be a whole word.
glossary.example: A space and word fragment may have their own tokenization.

glossary.definition: An unnormalized score for a possible next token.
glossary.example: Softmax turns all vocabulary logits into a probability distribution.

glossary.definition: A probability given specified information.
glossary.example: p(next token | prompt) changes when the prompt changes.

glossary.definition: The procedure that turns scores into tokens and decides when to stop.
glossary.example: Temperature and top-k form part of a sampling decoder.

glossary.definition: An intermediate numerical value produced during a forward pass.
glossary.example: The residual vector at the last prompt position in layer 12.

glossary.definition: A learned parameter used by the model’s computation.
glossary.example: A matrix that projects a residual vector into an attention query.

glossary.definition: The sequence of representations updated through additive connections.
glossary.example: Novel captures the decoder-block output after both residual additions.

glossary.definition: A learned operation that mixes value vectors using query-key compatibility weights.
glossary.example: A later position can use information from earlier permitted positions.

glossary.definition: Saved key and value states from previous positions, reused during decoding.
glossary.example: A retained perturbed cache preserves some effects after noise injection stops.

glossary.definition: Scoring a reference while supplying its preceding tokens instead of sampling them.
glossary.example: The final equation is scored after the reference derivation is already in the input.

glossary.definition: The precisely defined quantity an experiment aims to estimate.
glossary.example: Probability of valid target recovery for one frozen prompt and decoder.

glossary.definition: Sameness of the relevant meaning under stated assumptions and a rubric.
glossary.example: Renaming variables can preserve a mechanism; dropping a boundary condition may not.

glossary.definition: Whether the endorsed proposal solves the posed problem at the required evidence tier.
glossary.example: A correct older algorithm can count as valid.

glossary.definition: Whether the proposal contains the scoped historical target contribution.
glossary.example: The target’s particular memory schedule is present, not just its familiar algebra.

glossary.definition: The conjunction of validity and target mechanism match.
glossary.example: T is true only when both V and M are true.

glossary.definition: Evidence that the complete model condition predates the target’s first supported public contribution.
glossary.example: A July model snapshot cannot be certified with an April family launch alone.

glossary.definition: Information or selection that helps narrow the route to a solution.
glossary.example: Choosing two old inspirations based on a future paper is hindsight assistance.

glossary.definition: The probability that at least one of k candidates meets a success criterion, usually evaluated with an oracle.
glossary.example: A candidate pool can pass while an actual selector chooses its wrong member.

glossary.definition: A procedure with stated repeated-study coverage under assumptions.
glossary.example: A fixed-N binomial interval assumes the declared sampling model and reliable labels.

glossary.definition: Cases used to choose or revise the procedure.
glossary.example: A public worked historical case used for prompt design.

glossary.definition: Held-out cases evaluated using a prospectively frozen procedure.
glossary.example: A separately held contribution family that did not influence tuning.

glossary.definition: Whether an explanation accurately reflects influences on the computation being explained.
glossary.example: A trace may omit a hint that changed the answer.

glossary.definition: Replacing a specified internal state with another state during execution.
glossary.example: Copying one donor residual into an aligned recipient position.

glossary.definition: A vector used to change an activation or parameters according to a defined intervention.
glossary.example: Adding a scaled mean contrast to a residual state.

glossary.definition: Local derivatives of a scalar objective with respect to selected numbers.
glossary.example: A derivative of a target-logit contrast with respect to one residual vector.

glossary.definition: Removing or substituting part of a computation to test its effect.
glossary.example: Setting a selected component to a declared baseline and measuring output change.

glossary.definition: Evidence that supports a scoped scientific claim beyond operational correctness.
glossary.example: Human-adjudicated recovery under an admitted historical condition and frozen protocol.

glossary.definition: A list or rule assigning probabilities to all possible outcomes of a process.
glossary.example: The toy red/blue/stop distribution is 0.50/0.30/0.20.

glossary.definition: exp turns a real number into a positive number; the natural logarithm reverses it.
glossary.example: log(0.5) is about −0.693; exp(−0.693) is about 0.5.

glossary.definition: One number, an ordered list of numbers, and an array with any number of axes.
glossary.example: A hidden-state tensor with shape [1, 3, 4] stores 12 scalars.

glossary.definition: Multiply matching vector coordinates, then add the products to obtain one scalar.
A transformation forming weighted sums of input coordinates.
An execution of the model that computes activations and scores from inputs and current parameters.
glossary.example: The last prompt state produces scores for the next token.

glossary.definition: A scalar objective to minimize, and a rule that uses information such as derivatives to update parameters.
glossary.example: Computing an activation gradient without an optimizer step leaves the model weights fixed.

glossary.definition: A measure of how spread out a probability distribution is, relative to the specified outcomes or groups.
glossary.example: One meaning group has entropy zero, even if its claim is wrong.

glossary.definition: Trials sharing the same generating law, where learning previous outcomes does not change the next outcome’s distribution.
glossary.example: Frozen independent sampling is intended to support binomial inference; different seeds alone do not prove it.

glossary.definition: An alternative varying factor that could explain an observed relationship.
glossary.example: A positive/negative contrast that also changes answer length may mix task signal with length.

glossary.definition: A model predicting candidate outcomes, and a rule using that prediction and uncertainty to select the next candidate.
glossary.example: Adaptive perturbation search uses earlier verifier scores to choose another setting.

glossary.definition: A repeatable procedure for measuring a specified outcome.
glossary.example: Novel’s assay combines a historical challenge, generation settings and judgment of the resulting proposal.

glossary.definition: A relationship in which one statement being true is sufficient for another to be true in context.
glossary.example: Exactly two observations entails at least two; the reverse need not hold.

glossary.definition: Supervision supplies known labels or targets; a probe is an extra predictor trained to recover labels from model states.
